keyChanges.title: HW3 ECU thermal failures from FSD v14 Lite prompt emergency v14.1 Lite release (2026.21.6)
keyChanges.description: The most significant FSD software story of this research window is a hardware-level safety failure caused by the software stack. After Tesla pushed FSD v14 Lite wide-release (2026.20.6.11) to HW3 vehicles on July 21, a growing wave of owners reported Autopilot ECU overheating faults beginning in early August. Service-mode screenshots circulated on Tesla Motors Club and NotATeslaApp showing the APP_w141_ECU_Thermal_Issue fault triggering when board temperatures exceeded 90°C — the rated ceiling. Multiple owners documented temperatures of 96°C, some as high as 99–102°C. At 102°C, at least one owner reported the 'Start Self-Driving' button disappeared entirely, indicating the ECU had throttled out of FSD mode to protect itself. In the most severe cases, boards failed outright. The root cause is structural: the HW3 AI3 chip has 8GB of RAM and approximately one-eighth the memory bandwidth of HW4's AI4. FSD v14 Lite — a distilled version of the HW4 v14 neural net — pushes the AI3 chip harder than prior software generations, and the HW3 ECU sits at the top of the vehicle's coolant loop (farthest from the radiator), making it the most thermally vulnerable component. Tesla initially did not publicly acknowledge the issue. After approximately six weeks of internal testing, Tesla responded on August 8–9 by beginning rollout of FSD v14.1 Lite within software package 2026.21.6 — a revised build intended to reduce ECU thermal load on HW3 hardware. By August 15, the 2026.21.6 rollout had completed its 8th wave, reaching approximately 6,160+ additional vehicles. Critical reality: Tesla's first attempt at pushing a full-capability FSD model to HW3 hardware caused documented ECU thermal failures in the wild, requiring a same-cycle regression release. This is a hardware-ceiling problem that FSD v14.1 Lite partially addresses but does not eliminate. HW3 owners who suffered board failures face ambiguous warranty coverage, as Tesla had not acknowledged the software causation at time of reporting.

positive_signals: Tesla responded within approximately 6 weeks with v14.1 Lite (2026.21.6) specifically to address HW3 thermal load
2026.21.6 rollout was multi-wave and reached 6,160+ vehicles by August 15, showing active distribution
Tesla Oracle, NotATeslaApp, and TeslaNorth all corroborate the fix deployment timeline
negative_signals: FSD v14 Lite caused Autopilot ECU board temperatures to reach 96–102°C on HW3 vehicles, above the 90°C ceiling — documented by multiple owners with service-mode screenshots
At least some HW3 boards failed outright, leaving owners without FSD and facing potentially uncovered repair costs since Tesla had not acknowledged software causation
Tesla did not proactively acknowledge the thermal issue publicly before shipping the fix — affected owners were left to discover the fault themselves
v14.1 Lite is a downgraded capability build relative to v14 Lite; HW3 owners received a capability reduction as the 'fix' for a failure Tesla's own OTA caused

HW3 architecture (8GB RAM, one-eighth memory bandwidth of HW4, worst thermal position in coolant loop) makes it fundamentally unsuitable for the full v14 model — this is a structural ceiling problem, not a tuning issue

keyChanges.title: 2026.21.6 unified rollout delivers FSD v14.3.7 (HW4) + FSD v14.1 Lite (HW3) simultaneously
keyChanges.description: Software package 2026.21.6 began rolling out on August 8–9 as a unified dual-track release: FSD v14.3.7 for AI4/HW4 vehicles alongside FSD v14.1 Lite for AI3/HW3 vehicles. This is the first time Tesla has bundled separate HW3 and HW4 FSD builds into a single software package, signaling a more deliberate fleet-management approach to the capability ceiling divergence. For HW4 owners, v14.3.7 carries the same RL/MLIR/vision-encoder improvements documented in 2026.21.5 — brake-stutter regression fixed, highway-exit miss persisting, 20% faster reaction time from MLIR compiler rewrite. For HW3 owners, v14.1 Lite is a downscaled build that reduces ECU thermal load. Rollout statistics from NotATeslaApp show 803 cars (6.4% of FSD-enrolled fleet) on 2026.21.6 as of August 9, climbing with each wave. By August 15, an 8th wave had pushed to approximately 6,160 additional vehicles in a single window. At this pace, full HW4 fleet saturation of v14.3.7 remains weeks away. The 2026.26 Summer Update branch (non-FSD) rolled out separately; FSD-merged 2026.26.x waves are estimated for late August to early September. Critical reality: the dual-track distribution in 2026.21.6 confirms the permanent software divergence between HW3 and HW4 fleets — HW3 owners receive a capability-capped lite build, not the full production stack. The v14.3.7 branch itself represents point-release polish, not the architectural leap that v15 represents. Consumer v15 OTA remains a Q4 2026 / Q1 2027 target with no confirmed date.

positive_signals: 2026.21.6 unified rollout confirms Tesla actively managing HW3/HW4 software divergence in a coordinated single package
v14.3.7 brings confirmed brake-stutter fix from v14.3.6 regression plus MLIR compiler rewrite (20% faster reaction time)
Multi-wave rollout (8 waves by Aug 15) shows structured, monitored OTA distribution per notateslaapp.com statistics
negative_signals: HW3 owners receive v14.1 Lite — a capability reduction relative to v14 Lite, forced by thermal hardware constraints; this is a ceiling, not progress
v14.3.7 is a regression-patch point release; highway-exit miss from v14.3.6 reportedly still present
Fleet saturation still weeks away as of Aug 15; most consumers remain on the regressed v14.3.6 build
FSD-merged 2026.26 Summer Update (with any incremental FSD improvements) not expected until late August / early September at earliest
Consumer v15 OTA remains a Q4 2026 / Q1 2027 target — this research window produced zero new evidence of v15 progress or timeline pull-forward

keyChanges.title: FSD fleet crosses 13 billion cumulative miles; 1.5 million active users at 33M miles/day pace
keyChanges.description: Tesla's FSD (Supervised) fleet crossed 13 billion cumulative miles around August 3–4, 2026, per Basenor and an X.com data tracker. The most recent billion miles — from 12B to 13B — took approximately 17 days, reflecting a fleet-level cadence of roughly 33 million miles per day and approximately 1 billion miles every three weeks. The 12 billion milestone was reported July 17 (per TeslaNorth), making the 13B milestone a clean within-window development. Of the 13 billion total miles, 5 billion have been logged in urban environments — a key data quality metric for neural network training, since urban driving (intersections, pedestrians, cut-ins, construction) generates the dense edge-case scenarios most critical for FSD safety improvement. Active user count grew 56% year-over-year to 1.5 million monthly active users, consistent with FSD v14's broadly improved quality driving higher engagement per drive. Critical context: the accelerating mileage rate is a genuine positive for training data volume. However, Musk's own cited threshold of 10 billion miles for unsupervised readiness was crossed in May 2026 — and four months later, consumer unsupervised FSD remains a Q4 2026 target with no confirmed date. Raw mileage accumulation has clearly not been the sole binding constraint; software architecture (v15), regulatory approval, and liability framework remain the actual gatekeepers. The 13B milestone is a training-data input metric, not a readiness output metric.

positive_signals: Fleet logging 33 million miles/day — approximately 1 billion miles every three weeks — demonstrating accelerating data flywheel
5 billion of 13 billion total miles in urban environments, the highest-value training scenarios for edge-case safety
1.5 million active users (56% YoY growth) confirms FSD v14 quality improvements driving higher engagement and longer per-drive activation
negative_signals: Musk's 10 billion mile threshold for unsupervised readiness was crossed in May 2026 — three months later consumer unsupervised FSD is still Q4 2026 target at best, exposing the threshold as a non-binding heuristic
Mileage volume alone is not a release prerequisite; v15 architecture, regulatory framework, and geography-by-geography validation are the actual binding constraints
No new FSD safety report issued in this period to substantiate whether the additional training miles are producing measurable safety metric improvements

categoryUpdate.latestStatus: FSD v14.3.7 in slow fleet rollout (6.4% HW4 fleet as of Aug 9 per NotATeslaApp) via 2026.21.6 unified package. HW3 owners received FSD v14.1 Lite as thermal-failure fix; HW3 hardware ceiling now confirmed as structural. Consumer v15 OTA remains Q4 2026/Q1 2027 target — no new evidence of schedule pull-forward. FSD-merged Summer Update (2026.26.x) expected late August/early September.
categoryUpdate.nextMilestone: FSD-merged 2026.26 Summer Update (late August / early September 2026); consumer FSD v15 OTA (Q4 2026 / Q1 2027 at earliest)
concerns: HW3 ECU thermal failures caused by FSD v14 Lite OTA represent a software-induced hardware damage event — Tesla's liability exposure if boards are failing under warranty is unresolved
v14.3.7 is still a point-release regression patch; no new capabilities; highway-exit miss persists
Consumer v15 timeline remains vague — 'end of 2026 or early 2027' has not tightened despite robotaxi fleet already running early v15 builds
FSD-merged Summer Update (2026.26.x) is a branch merge, not a new FSD capability version; investor expectations for a Q3 software milestone may be disappointed
HW3 software divergence is now permanent: v14.1 Lite is not the full v14 stack, and HW3 will never receive v15 — affecting ~2 million vehicles and their FSD subscription revenue
